name: Bengali
catalog_quote: (11) Word Stress — Stress the initial syllable of a word. This rule is inviolable.
sweep_summary: Bengali (beng1280) is in the catalog as fixed-strict initial (Hayes & Lahiri 1991:55). The sweep had one item, Khan's 2008 UCLA dissertation on Bengali intonation; an open author copy was found on his Reed College page and fetched sources (the PDF text layer is garbled, so section 6 'Stress', pp. 20-34, was scanned at 250 dpi). Khan reviews all prior stress work and concludes that primary stress is initial, non-contrastive and phonetically weak but phonologically salient (lax/nasal vowel distribution, loanword truncation, syncope, metathesis, enclitic alternations, pitch-accent attraction), with frequent secondary stress on later odd syllables; he notes two minority weight-sensitive analyses (Shaw 1984 second-syllable stress unless the first is closed; Das 2001 for Tripura Bengali) and a loanword exception for some speakers (fn. 11). This confirms the catalog coding and does not supersede Hayes & Lahiri 1991, which remains the deciding statement; Khan 2008 is a strong corroborating source and supplies the literature map. Two further open copies were found and read on the same page: Khan 2010 JIPA illustration (p. 223: 'consistently word-initial') and Khan 2014 Prosodic Typology II chapter (p. 84 + fn. 3), the latter previously recorded as paywalled in REF_UNIVERSE. nothing remains unread.

new_statements.quote: Although stress in Bengali appears to be phonetically weak, it is nevertheless phonologically salient. Bengali clearly does assign a special status to particular syllables, whose properties are roughly equivalent to the non-phonetic correlates of stress in English. This special status is always a property of the initial syllable of native monomorphemic words, and normally also on borrowings and complex words. There is often a similar status on all odd-numbered syllables after the initial syllable. [fn. 11:] Primary stress is nearly always word-initial; however, some words borrowed from Perso-Arabic, English, or Sanskrit can bear non-initial primary stress in some speakers' pronunciations.
new_statements.citation: Khan, Sameer ud Dowla. 2008. Intonational phonology and focus prosody of Bengali. Ph.D. dissertation, UCLA.
new_statements.locator: sec. 6.4, p. 25 (PDF p. 60), with fn. 11; cf. sec. 6.6 summary p. 33 (PDF p. 68)
new_statements.reading: Primary word stress is fixed on the initial syllable (with optional secondary stresses on later odd-numbered syllables); it is non-contrastive and phonetically weak but phonologically real, shown by vowel-quality/nasality restrictions, syncope, metathesis, enclitic hiatus and pitch-accent attraction. The only qualifications are speaker-variable non-initial stress in some Perso-Arabic/English/Sanskrit loans (fn. 11) and two minority weight-sensitive analyses (Shaw 1984; Das 2001 for Tripura Bengali) that Khan reports but does not adopt. This confirms the catalog's fixed-strict initial coding and its WORD domain; it refines the picture by documenting secondary stress and the loanword exception.

audit.reasoning: Quote verified verbatim at the stated page (Hayes & Lahiri 1991:55) in the held PDF. The deciding source is the standard specialist phonology article for Bengali prosody, and two further held specialist sources (Khan 2008 UCLA diss. pp. 22-23, surveying ten prior descriptions; Khan 2010 JIPA Illustration p. 222) independently state consistent word-initial, non-contrastive stress, matching the catalog's fixed-strict initial coding (rule '10 100 1000...'). No held or found source contradicts; the only dissent (Shaw 1984, Das 2001 on Tripura Bangla, weight-sensitive) is minority, partly dialectal, and reported by Khan as lacking acoustic support — at most worth a one-line caution, not a recode. Nothing was fetched sources (no open copy of a better source exists; the best sources are already held). sources.quote: "For Bengali, word stress follows a very simple rule (cf. Chatterji 1921, Klaiman 1987): (11) Word Stress — Stress the initial syllable of a word. This rule is inviolable. Compound words also have their strongest stress on their initial syllables. There may also be a weaker stress on the initial syllable of their second member, but this is hard to hear." (p. 55)

sources.citation: Khan, Sameer ud Dowla. 2008. Intonational phonology and focus prosody of Bengali. Ph.D. dissertation, University of California, Los Angeles. (Glottolog 627451)
sources.quote: It is claimed in nearly all studies (Chatterji 1921, Goswami 1944, Ferguson & Chowdhury 1960, Anderson 1962, Bykova 1981, Kawasaki & Shattuck-Hufnagel 1988, Hayes & Lahiri 1991, Lahiri & Fitzpatrick-Cole 1999, Michaels & Nelson 2004; Selkirk 2006) that words are consistently stressed on the initial syllable [...]. Only two studies, to my knowledge, claim that stress can occur on non-initial syllables. Shaw (1984) claims that stress is assigned to the second syllable [...], unless the first syllable is heavy (i.e. closed) [...]. Das (2001) [...] also claims that the stress pattern of both Tripuri Bengali and Standard Bengali is quantity-sensitive. (pp. 22-23)
sources.locator: ch. 2 sec. 6 'Stress', pp. 20-34 (word stress 6.1 pp. 21-23; phonological correlates 6.4 pp. 25-31 with fn. 11 p. 25; summary 6.6 pp. 33-34); PDF page = diss. page + 35
sources.note: The dissertation is mainly about intonation, but ch. 2 sec. 6 is a first-hand review and analysis of Bengali word stress. Word stress is non-contrastive and phonetically weak (Kawasaki & Shattuck-Hufnagel 1988 found no reliable F0/intensity cue), but phonologically salient: 'This special status is always a property of the initial syllable of native monomorphemic words, and normally also on borrowings and complex words' (p. 25), with secondary stress often on odd-numbered syllables after the initial one (p. 25). Evidence: lax and nasal vowels confined to stressed syllables, loanword truncation…

sources.quote: Pitch accents are tones that attach to the most metrically prominent syllable in the AP; in Bengali, which does not have lexically contrastive stress, this is consistently the word-initial syllable. [fn. 3:] While the majority of studies of Bengali agree that stress is consistently word-initial, some studies claim otherwise. See Khan (2008) §6 for a review of the literature on Bengali stress as well as for a new phonological analysis of stress in Bengali. (p. 84)
sources.note: Intonation chapter; states in passing that Bengali has no contrastive stress but 'predictable stress assignment' (p. 81) and that the pitch accent docks on the consistently word-initial stressed syllable (p. 84), deferring the stress argument to Khan 2008 sec. 6.

sources.citation: Khan, Sameer ud Dowla. 2010. Bengali (Bangladeshi Standard). Journal of the International Phonetic Association 40(2): 221-225. DOI 10.1017/S0025100310000071. [not in the sweep list; found on the author's page during this sweep]
sources.quote: Stress is not marked in broad transcription as it is consistently word-initial. While stress is neither contrastive nor phonetically salient (Chatterji 1921, Goswami 1944, Ferguson & Chowdhury 1960, Anderson 1962, Bykova 1981, Kawasaki & Shattuck-Hufnagel 1988, Hayes & Lahiri 1991, Lahiri & Fitzpatrick-Cole 1999, Michaels & Nelson 2004, Selkirk 2006), it is associated with phonological alternations and plays an important role in the intonational system, as it is associated with the postlexical pitch accent (Khan 2008: chapter 2).
sources.note: Consistently word-initial, non-contrastive, phonetically weak but phonologically active; the IPA Illustration for Bangladeshi Standard Bengali.
